title: High-Risk Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (HR-PDR)
summary: High-Risk PDR represents a critical threshold in diabetic eye disease where the risk of severe vision loss (SVL) increases exponentially. This guide covers the landmark DRS criteria, multimodal imaging, and the evolving paradigm of PRP vs. Anti-VEGF therapy.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Significance
sections.content: Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) is characterized by the presence of extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation. 'High-Risk' PDR is a specific subset defined by the Diabetic Retinopathy Study (DRS) as having a high risk of developing severe visual loss (defined as visual acuity <5/200 on two consecutive visits) within 2 years if left untreated.

rows: Neovascularization at or within 1DD of the optic disc.
Any NVD associated with Vitreous Hemorrhage (VH) or Preretinal Hemorrhage (PRH).
Neovascularization elsewhere ≥ 0.5 disc area AND VH or PRH.
Large area of ischemia and active bleeding.
Vitreous or Preretinal hemorrhage associated with NVD or NVE.
The hallmark of proliferative activity and risk.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Ischemic Cascade
content: 1. Chronic Hyperglycemia: Leads to polyol pathway activation and AGE accumulation.
2. Capillary Non-perfusion: Pericyte loss and basement membrane thickening cause microvascular occlusion.
3. Retinal Hypoxia: Triggered by extensive capillary dropout.
4. Cytokine Release: Upregulation of VEGF (Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor) and Erythropoietin.
5. Neovascularization: New vessels lack tight junctions, leading to leakage and tractional membranes.

rows: Hemisheaths, sudden onset, optic disc swelling in CRVO.
Pain, mid-peripheral blot hemes, narrowed arteries.
History of plaque or external beam radiation.

branches: FFA: Identifying areas of capillary non-perfusion (CNP) and leakage at NVD/NVE
OCT-Macula: Evaluate for concomitant DME (Diabetic Macular Edema)
OCT-A: Non-invasive detection of FVP and foveal avascular zone (FAZ) enlargement
B-Scan USG: Critical if VH obscures fundus; rule out Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD)
Wide-field Imaging: Captures peripheral ischemia and NVE outside standard 7-fields

sections.title: Management Algorithm: Treatment of Choice
content: Step 1: Systemic Optimization (HbA1c < 7.0%, BP < 130/80, Lipid control).
Step 2: Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP) - Gold Standard. 1200-1500 burns, 200-500um spot, 0.1s duration.
Step 3: Intravitreal Anti-VEGF (Ranibizumab/Aflibercept) - Non-inferior to PRP for VA (Protocol S), but requires high compliance.
Step 4: Combination Therapy - Anti-VEGF prior to PRP to reduce DME risk and facilitate NV regression.
Step 5: Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) - Indicated for non-clearing VH, TRD, or combined RRD/TRD.

sections.title: Surgical Indications & Red Flags
content: Non-clearing Vitreous Hemorrhage (>1 month in T1DM, >3 months in T2DM)
Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD) involving or threatening the macula
Combined Tractional and Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment
Neovascular Glaucoma (NVG) with media opacity preventing PRP
Ghost Cell Glaucoma

content.explanation: High risk of PDR progression: 4 quadrants of severe hemorrhages, 2 quadrants of venous beading, or 1 quadrant of IRMA.

rows: PRP reduces risk of SVL by >50%.
Established PRP as standard of care.
PRP not recommended for mild/mod NPDR; consider in severe NPDR/early PDR.
Ranibizumab non-inferior to PRP through 5 years for visual acuity.
Alternative to laser in compliant patients.
Aflibercept superior to PRP for VA outcomes at 1 year.
Anti-VEGF prevents PDR in high-risk NPDR.

sections.title: PRP Technical Pearls
content: Burn intensity: Dull white/grey (Level II-III).
Spacing: One burn width apart.
Extent: From vascular arches to the periphery.
Avoid: Direct treatment of the macula, major vessels, or optic disc.
Retrobulbar block: Consider if patient is sensitive or for extensive supplementation.

sections.title: Vitreoretinal Surgery Steps
content: 1. 23G or 25G Valved Trocar Placement.
2. Core Vitrectomy and induction of PVD (if not present).
3. Segmentation/Delamination of fibrovascular membranes.
4. Hemostasis using endodiathermy.
5. Endolaser Photocoagulation (Filling in PRP gaps).
6. Fluid-Air Exchange and optional Silicone Oil/Gas Tamponade.

branches: PRP: Constriction of visual field, night blindness, choroidal effusion
Surgery: Iatrogenic breaks, recurrence of VH, cataract progression

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always rule out Neovascular Glaucoma; perform gonioscopy on all HR-PDR patients.
Treat DME before or concurrent with PRP to prevent laser-induced maculopathy.
Falsely low HbA1c: Check for sickle cell, anemia, or recent transfusions.
Pregnancy can cause rapid acceleration of PDR; requires monthly screening.
Post-PRP VH: Doesn't always mean failure; may be 'washout' of old heme.
